text: Generative AI for game development, ethical and practical considerations. The guardrails that keep AI stories human. Hello, this is Liam in for Bear. Some developers treat ethics as a speed bump paperwork before the real work. This chapter argues the opposite. The guardrails are what make AI stories worth telling. Six terms then we're off. Bias, inherited stereotypes in generated content. Authorship, who owns what the AI wrote. Hallucination, confident falsehoods. Emotional safety, no jarring content. Data privacy, player input stays private. Over-reliance, convenience that flattens the story. When you put AI in your story, you're not just generating text. You're building a system that speaks to people, interprets their input, and makes

Creative decisions on their behalf at scale in real time. Ethical means five things. Inclusive, represent diverse identities. Emotionally aware, respect the tone. Transparent, players know what's AI. Accountable, someone owns the output. Story first, serve the narrative not the content quota. Three questions to carry through this chapter. What values are we encoding? Whose voices are we amplifying or silencing? And how do we protect players from harm without silencing difficult topics? Bias, models are trained on the internet and the internet has opinions. Ask for a doctor and a nurse and the old models defaulted to male doctors, female nurses. No intent required. The fix is fine-tune on bias-aware data sets. Have

Writers review generated content. Use neutral templates. Assign roles randomly unless the story constrains them. Let players customize characters out of the defaults. Authorship, when the AI writes your game's most powerful scene, who owns it? The line between tool and collaborator blurs and credit, accountability, and creative identity blur with it. Make it transparent. Credit AI contributions in your dev log. Tag scenes AI-generated, edited, or human-authored. Require editorial review before anything ships. Set a clear internal IP policy. Coherence, you bond with an NPC for hours, then the AI forgets. The relationship evaporates, the illusion collapses, and what felt real now feels mechanical. Protect continuity. Use AI for filler,

Not foundational scenes. Track decisions as variables. Write fallback dialogues for when the model slips. Limit the AI's memory scope deliberately. Hallucination, the AI confidently invents a place that doesn't exist, a dead character walking around, lore that contradicts your world. In fiction, it breaks immersion. In grounded settings, it can misrepresent real cultures. Ground it, feed the model a lore Bible with RAG. Constrain it, use only canonical facts, require human review of critical beats. Run consistency checkers and adversarial QA prompts designed to break it. Trust, players attach to your characters. When the AI swerves into dark or traumatic content unprompted, as early AI Dungeon did, that attachment turns to harm.

Guard the tone, bake tone instructions into every prompt. Run content filters post generation. Let players choose optimistic, neutral, or dark, and give them a way to flag what crosses the line. Privacy, your narrative system invites players to write journal entries, confessions, fears. If that text goes to an external API, you've built a surveillance device with a story attached. Keep it local and consensual. Process sensitive input on device. Show a clear processed by AI notice with opt out. Anonymize before sending. Purge conversations after the session. Over-reliance, the convenience trap. AI fills every gap, side quests, lore, dialogue, until the story feels generated, smooth, generic, and emotionally flat. AI assists, writers

Decide. Generate 10 quest hooks, let the human pick one. Mark AI scenes in the story Bible. Keep a thematic checklist, and give writers veto power over anything that doesn't meet the bar. The developer checklist seven categories, bias and representation, authorship and transparency, narrative coherence, player safety, data privacy, creative oversight, intentional design, run it at planning during development, and a content review. What the AI can't do, lived experience, intuition, emotional memory. It can imitate human truth well enough to fool you, but the story still needs someone who's actually lived. Ethical storytelling in the age of AI isn't a constraint. It's an opportunity to tell better stories with more nuance, more

Responsibility, and more impact than ever before. The guardrails in six lines. One, bias is inherited, review and randomize. Two, authorship must be transparent, tag and credit. Three, coherence needs variables and fallbacks. Four, hallucinations need grounding, RAG and constraints. Five, protect tone and privacy by design. Six, AI assists writers decide. Your turn, pick one AI-driven feature in your game, a dialogue generator, a quest writer, anything. Run it through the seven checklist categories and write down one concrete guardrail for each. Ethical and practical considerations at Nick Bear Brown.
